subtopic: Solubility and Capacity to Dissolve Solute
stem: The solubility of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas in water at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 1 bar is \(6.85 \times 10^{-4}\) \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\). Calculate (a) Henry's law constant (b) molarity of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas dissolved in water under atmospheric conditions when partial pressure of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) in atmosphere is 0.75 bar.
solution:
a. \(\mathrm{K_H} = \dfrac{S}{P} = \dfrac{6.85 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}}{1\ \mathrm{bar}} = 6.85 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}}\)

b. \(S = \mathrm{K_H}P = 6.85 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}} \times 0.75\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(= 5.138 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

subtopic: Solubility and Capacity to Dissolve Solute
stem: The Henry's law constant of methyl bromide \(\mathrm{(CH_3Br)}\), is 0.159 \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}}\) at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\). What is the solubility of methyl bromide in water at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and at pressure of 130 mmHg?
solution:
According to Henry's law

\(S = \mathrm{K_H}P\)

1. \(\mathrm{K_H} = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}}\)

2. \(P = 130\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times \dfrac{1}{760\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg/atm}}\)

\(= 0.171\ \mathrm{atm} \times 1.013\ \mathrm{bar/atm} = 0.173\ \mathrm{bar}\)

Hence, \(S = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}} \times 0.173\ \mathrm{bar} = 0.0275\ \mathrm{M}\)

subtopic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions of Liquids in Liquids
stem: The vapour pressures of pure liquids A and B are 450 mm Hg and 700 mm Hg, respectively at 350 K. Find the composition of liquid and vapour if total vapour pressure is 600 mm.
solution:
i. Compositions of A and B in the solution are \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)

\(P = (P_2^0 - P_1^0)x_2 + P_1^0\)

\(P_1^0 = 450\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ P_2^0 = 700\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ P = 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

Hence, \(600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} = (700\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} - 450\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg})x_2 + 450\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} = 250x_2 + 450\)

\(600 - 450 = 150 = 250x_2\) or \(x_2 = \dfrac{150}{250} = 0.6\)

\(x_1 = 1 - x_2 = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4\)

ii. Compositions of A and B in vapour are \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) respectively.

\(P_1 = y_1P\) and \(P_2 = y_2P\), \(P_1 = P_1^0x_1\) and \(P_2 = P_2^0x_2\)

\(y_1 = \dfrac{P_1}{P} = \dfrac{P_1^0x_1}{P} = \dfrac{450\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 0.4}{600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}} = 0.3\)

\(y_2 = 1 - y_1 = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7\)

stem: A solution is prepared by dissolving 394 g of a nonvolatile solute in 622 g of water. The vapour pressure of solution is found to be 30.74 mm Hg at \(30^\circ\mathrm{C}\). If vapour pressure of water at \(30^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is 31.8 mm Hg, what is the molar mass of solute?
solution:
\(\dfrac{P_1^0 - P_1}{P_1^0} = \dfrac{\Delta P}{P_1^0} = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}M_1}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(\mathrm{W_2} = 394\ \mathrm{g},\ \mathrm{W_1} = 622\ \mathrm{g},\ M_1 = 18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\),

\(P_1 = 30.74\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ P_1^0 = 31.8\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

Substitution of these quantities into the equation gives

\(\dfrac{31.8\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} - 30.74\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}}{31.8\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}} = \dfrac{394\ \mathrm{g} \times 18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{M_2 \times 622\ \mathrm{g}}\)

\(0.0333 = \dfrac{11.4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{M_2}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{11.4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{0.0333} = 342\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem: The vapour pressure of pure benzene (molar mass 78 g/mol) at a certain temperature is 640 mm Hg. A nonvolatile solute of mass 2.315 g is added to 49 g of benzene. The vapour pressure of the solution is 600 mm Hg. What is the molar mass of solute?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed working sets a MINUS sign where a multiplication sign belongs, writing "2.315 g - 78 g/mol" in all three lines that carry the numerator. Read literally that is \(-75.685\) and cannot produce the book's own answer; 58.96 follows only from \(2.315 \times 78 \times 640/(40 \times 49)\). The operator has been corrected below, and the final unit, printed as "g mol", restored to \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\). The answer 58.96 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) is correct.]

\(\dfrac{P_1^0 - P_1}{P_1^0} = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2} \times M_1}{M_2 \times \mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(P_1^0 = 640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ P_1 = 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ \mathrm{W_1} = 49\ \mathrm{g},\ \mathrm{W_2} = 2.315\ \mathrm{g}\)

Hence, \(\dfrac{640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} - 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}}{640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}} = \dfrac{2.315\ \mathrm{g} \times 78\ \mathrm{g/mol}}{49\ \mathrm{g} \times M_2}\)

\(\dfrac{40\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}}{640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}} = \dfrac{2.315\ \mathrm{g} \times 78\ \mathrm{g/mol}}{49\ \mathrm{g} \times M_2}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{2.315\ \mathrm{g} \times 78\ \mathrm{g/mol} \times 640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}}{40\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 49\ \mathrm{g}} = 58.96\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem: The normal boiling point of ethyl acetate is \(77.06^\circ\mathrm{C}\). A solution of 50 g of a nonvolatile solute in 150 g of ethyl acetate boils at \(84.27^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Evaluate the molar mass of solute if \(\mathrm{K_b}\) for ethyl acetate is \(2.77^\circ\mathrm{C\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(\mathrm{W_2} = 50\ \mathrm{g},\ \mathrm{W_1} = 150\ \mathrm{g}\),

\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0 = 84.27^\circ\mathrm{C} - 77.06^\circ\mathrm{C} = 7.21^\circ\mathrm{C} = 7.21\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(K_b = 2.77^\circ\mathrm{C\ kg\ mol^{-1}} = 2.77\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\)

Substitution of these in above equation

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{g\ kg^{-1}} \times 2.77\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 50\ \mathrm{g}}{7.21\ \mathrm{K} \times 150\ \mathrm{g}} = 128\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem: 3.795 g of sulphur is dissolved in 100 g of carbon disulphide. This solution boils at 319.81 K. What is the molecular formula of sulphur in solution? The boiling point of the solvent is 319.45 K. (Given that \(K_b\) for \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) = 2.42 \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\) and atomic mass of S = 32 u
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed working gives \(255.1/32 = 7.92\); the division is 7.97. The conclusion is unaffected, since both round to 8 and the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{S_8}\), so the printed value is preserved below. The stem also opens a parenthesis before "Given that" which is never closed.]

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(\mathrm{W_1} = 100\ \mathrm{g},\ \mathrm{W_2} = 3.795\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(\Delta T_b = (319.81 - 319.45)\ \mathrm{K} = 0.36\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{g\ kg^{-1}} \times 2.42\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 3.795\ \mathrm{g}}{0.36\ \mathrm{K} \times 100\ \mathrm{g}} = 255.10\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Atomic mass of S = 32 u

Therefore number of atoms in a molecule of sulphur

\(= \dfrac{\text{molar mass of S}}{\text{atomic mass of S}} = \dfrac{255.1}{32} = 7.92 \approx 8\)

The molecular formula would be \(\mathrm{S_8}\) in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\)

stem: 1.02 g of urea when dissolved in 98.5 g of certain solvent decreases its freezing point by 0.211 K. 1.609 g of unknown compound when dissolved in 86 g of the same solvent depresses the freezing point by 0.34 K. Calculate the molar mass of the unknown compound. (Molar mass of urea = 60 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\))
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the working establishes \(1222.55 = M_2' \times 18.173\) and then divides by 18.175 on the next line. The two differ in the last digit only and both give \(M_2' = 67.3\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), so the answer is unaffected and the printed values are preserved below.]

| | Urea | Unknown compound |
|---|---|---|
| mass of solute | \(\mathrm{W_2} = 1.02\) g | \(\mathrm{W_2}' = 1.609\) g |
| mass of solvent | \(\mathrm{W_1} = 98.5\) g | \(\mathrm{W_1}' = 86\) g |
| freezing point depression | \(\Delta T_f = 0.211\) K | \(\Delta T_f' = 0.34\) K |
| molar mass | \(M_2 = 60\) \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) | \(M_2' = ?\) |

\(1000K_f = \dfrac{M_2 \times \Delta T_f \times \mathrm{W_1}}{\mathrm{W_2}} = \dfrac{M_2' \times \Delta T_f' \times \mathrm{W_1}'}{\mathrm{W_2}'}\)

\(= \dfrac{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.211\ \mathrm{K} \times 98.5\ \mathrm{g}}{1.02\ \mathrm{g}} = \dfrac{M_2' \times 0.34\ \mathrm{K} \times 86\ \mathrm{g}}{1.609\ \mathrm{g}}\)

\(\dfrac{1247.01\ \mathrm{g\ K\ mol^{-1}}}{1.02} = \dfrac{M_2' \times 29.24\ \mathrm{K}}{1.609}\)

\(1222.55\ \mathrm{g\ K\ mol^{-1}} = M_2' \times 18.173\)

\(M_2' = \dfrac{1222.55\ \mathrm{g\ K\ mol^{-1}}}{18.175\ \mathrm{K}} = 67.3\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem: What is the molar mass of a solute if a solution prepared by dissolving 0.822 g of it in 300 \(\mathrm{mdm^3}\) of water has an osmotic pressure of 149 mm Hg at 298 K?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the stem prints the volume as "300 \(\mathrm{mdm^3}\)", which is not a unit. The book's own solution uses \(V = 300\ \mathrm{mL} = 0.3\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), and that is the value from which the answer 342 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) follows.]

\(M_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{\pi V}\)

\(\mathrm{W_2} = 0.822\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(R = 0.08205\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(\pi = 149\ \mathrm{(mmHg)} = \dfrac{149\ \mathrm{(mmHg)}}{760\ \mathrm{(mmHg/atm)}} = 0.196\ \mathrm{atm}\)

\(V = 300\ \mathrm{mL} = 0.3\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{0.822\ \mathrm{g} \times 0.08205\ \mathrm{L\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K}}{0.196\ \mathrm{atm} \times 0.3\ \mathrm{dm^3}} = 342\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem: 0.2 \(m\) aqueous solution of KCl freezes at \(-0.680^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Calculate van't Hoff factor and osmotic pressure of solution at \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\). \((\mathrm{K_f} = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}})\)
solution:
\(\Delta T_f = K_f m\)

\(\Delta T_f = 0.680\ \mathrm{K},\ m = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

\((\Delta T_f)_0 = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}} = 0.372\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(i = \dfrac{(\Delta T_f)}{(\Delta T_f)_0} = \dfrac{0.680\ \mathrm{K}}{0.372\ \mathrm{K}} = 1.83\)

\((\pi)_0 = MRT = \dfrac{n_2}{V}RT\)

\(= \dfrac{0.2\ \mathrm{mol} \times 0.08205\ \mathrm{L\ atm\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}} \times 273\ \mathrm{K}}{1\ \mathrm{L}} = 4.48\ \mathrm{atm}\)

\(i = 1.83 = \dfrac{\pi}{\pi_0}\)

\(\pi = 1.83 \times 4.48\ \mathrm{atm}\)

\(\pi = 8.2\ \mathrm{atm}\)

stem: \(0.01m\) aqueous formic acid solution freezes at \(-0.021^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Calculate its degree of dissociation. \(\mathrm{K_f} = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\)
solution:
\(\Delta T_f = i\,\mathrm{K_f}m\)

\(\Delta T_f = 0^\circ\mathrm{C} - (-0.021^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 0.021^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

\(m = 0.01\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

\(0.021 = i \times 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.01\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

\(i = \dfrac{0.021}{1.86 \times 0.01} = 1.13\)

\(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1} = i - 1\) because \(n = 2\)

Hence, \(\alpha = 1.13 - 1 = 0.13 = 13\%\)

stem: 3.4 g of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) is dissolved in 2.5 L of water at 300 K. What is the osmotic pressure of the solution? van't Hoff factor for \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) is 2.47.
solution:
\(\pi = iMRT = i\dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{M_2V}\)

\(i = 2.47,\ \mathrm{W_2} = 3.4\ \mathrm{g},\ R = 0.08206\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}},\ T = 300\ \mathrm{K},\ M_2 = 40 + 71 = 111\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}},\ V = 2.5\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

\(\pi = 2.47 \times \dfrac{3.4\ \mathrm{g} \times 0.08206\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 300\ \mathrm{K}}{111\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} \times 2.5\ \mathrm{dm^3}} = 0.745\ \mathrm{atm}\)

stem: Which of following solutions will have maximum boiling point elevation and which have minimum freezing point depression assuming the complete dissociation? (a) 0.1 \(m\) KCl (b) 0.05 \(m\) NaCl (c) \(1m\) \(\mathrm{AlPO_4}\) (d) 0.1 \(m\) \(\mathrm{MgSO_4}\)
solution:
Boiling point elevation and freezing point depression are colligative properties that depend on number of particles in solution. The solution having more number of particles will have large boiling point elevation and that having less number of particles would show minimum freezing point depression.

(a) \(\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\); 0.1m, 0.1m, 0.1m — Total particles in solution = 0.2 mol

(b) \(\mathrm{NaCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\); 0.05m, 0.05m, 0.05m — Total particles in solution = 0.1 mol

(c) \(\mathrm{AlPO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}} + \mathrm{PO_4^{3\ominus}}\); 1m, 1m, 1m — Total particles in solution = 2.0 mol

(d) \(\mathrm{MgSO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\); 0.1m, 0.1m, 0.1m — Total particles in solution = 0.2 mole

\(\mathrm{AlPO_4}\) solution contains highest moles and hence highest number particles and in turn, the maximum \(\Delta T_b\). NaCl solution has minimum moles and particles. It has minimum \(\Delta T_f\).

stem: Assuming complete dissociation, calculate the molality of an aqueous solution of KBr whose freezing point is \(-2.95^\circ\mathrm{C}\). \(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water is 1.86 \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\)
solution:
\(\mathrm{KBr} = \mathrm{K^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\),

\(i = \dfrac{\text{moles of particles after dissociation}}{\text{moles of particles dissolved}} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\)

\(\Delta T_f = iK_f m\)

\(\Delta T_f = 0^\circ\mathrm{C} - (-2.95^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 2.95^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

\(m = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{iK_f} = \dfrac{2.95\ \mathrm{K}}{2 \times 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.793\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)
